(4) A reference in this section to an offence against an environmental law does not include an offence against Part VIIA of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 (compulsory pilotage).

section.heading: Power to conduct a frisk search of an arrested person

content.p: An authorised officer who arrests a person for an offence against an environmental law, or who is present at such an arrest, may, if the authorised officer suspects on reasonable grounds that it is prudent to do so in order to ascertain whether the arrested person is carrying any eligible seizable items:
conduct a frisk search of the arrested person at or soon after the time of arrest; and
seize any eligible seizable items found as a result of the search.

section.heading: Power to conduct an ordinary search of an arrested person

content.p: An authorised officer who arrests a person for an offence against an environmental law, or who is present at such an arrest, may, if the authorised officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the arrested person is carrying:
evidential material in relation to that or another offence against an environmental law; or
evidential material in relation to a contravention of an environmental penalty provision; or
an eligible seizable item;
conduct an ordinary search of the arrested person at or soon after the time or arrest, and seize any such thing found as a result of the search.

section.heading: Power to conduct search of arrested person’s premises

content.p: An authorised officer who arrests a person at premises for an offence against an environmental law, or who is present at such an arrest, may seize a thing in plain view at those premises that the authorised officer believes on reasonable grounds to be:
evidential material in relation to that or another offence against an environmental law; or
evidential material in relation to a contravention of an environmental penalty provision; or
an eligible seizable item.

section.heading: Interaction of this Division with Schedule 1

content.p: This Division does not limit, and is not limited by, Schedule 1. In particular, the detention of a person under Schedule 1 is not to be taken to constitute the arrest of the person for the purposes of this Division.

division.heading: Provisions relating to detention of suspected foreign offenders

section.heading: Provisions relating to detention of suspected foreign offenders

content.p: Schedule 1 has effect.

division.heading: Miscellaneous provisions about searches, entry to premises, warrants etc.

section.heading: Conduct of ordinary searches and frisk searches

content.p: An ordinary search or a frisk search of a person under this Part must, if practicable, be conducted by a person of the same sex as the person being searched.

section.heading: Announcement before entry

content.p: An authorised officer must, before any person enters premises under a warrant or to arrest a person under this Act:
announce that he or she is authorised to enter the premises; and
give any person at the premises an opportunity to allow entry to the premises.
An authorised officer is not required to comply with subsection (1) if he or she believes on reasonable grounds that immediate entry to the premises is required to ensure:
the safety of a person (including an authorised officer); or
that the effective execution of the warrant or the arrest is not frustrated.

section.heading: Offence of making false statements in warrants

content.p: A person commits an offence punishable upon conviction by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years if the person:
makes a statement in an application for a warrant; and
does so knowing the statement is false or misleading in a material particular.

section.heading: Offences relating to telephone warrants

content.p: A person must not:
state in a document that purports to be a form of warrant under section 409A or 416 the name of a magistrate unless the magistrate issued the warrant; or
state on a form of warrant under section 409A or 416 a matter that, to the person’s knowledge, departs in a material particular from the form authorised by the magistrate; or
purport to execute, or present to another person, a document that purports to be a form of warrant under section 409A or 416 that the person knows:
has not been approved by a magistrate under that section; or
departs in a material particular from the terms authorised by a magistrate under that section; or
give to a magistrate a form of warrant under section 409A or 416 that is not the form of warrant that the person purported to execute.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years.

section.heading: Retention of things seized under Division 4 or 6

content.p: This section applies to a thing that is seized under Division 4 or 6.
(2) The thing may be retained until:
the reason for the seizure of the thing no longer exists; or
it is decided that the thing is not to be used in evidence;
whichever happens first.

As soon as practicable after the end of the period during which the thing may be retained under subsection (2), the CEO must cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
Subsection (3) does not apply if:
the thing is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth; or

the thing has been dealt with under this Part, or as otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory), in a way that means the CEO is not in a position to cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing; or

the Commonwealth, the CEO or an authorised officer is otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory) to retain, destroy, dispose of or otherwise deal with the thing.

section.heading: Law relating to legal professional privilege not affected

content.p: This Part does not affect the law relating to legal professional privilege.

section.heading: Other laws about search, arrest etc. not affected

content.p: This Part is not intended to limit or exclude the operation of another law of the Commonwealth relating to:
the search of persons or premises; or
arrest and related matters; or
the stopping, detaining or searching of aircraft, vehicles or vessels; or
the seizure of things.

To avoid doubt, it is declared that even though another law of the Commonwealth provides power to do one or more of the things referred to in subsection (1), a similar power conferred by this Part may be used despite the existence of the power under the other law.

section.heading: Persons to assist authorised officers

content.p: Subject to subsection (5), the owner, or person in charge:
of any vehicle, vessel, aircraft or platform boarded by an authorised officer under section 403; or
of any premises entered by an authorised officer under section 405;

must, if requested by an authorised officer to do so, provide reasonable assistance to the authorised officer in the performance of the functions, or carrying out of the duties, or the exercise of the powers, conferred on the authorised officer under this Act.
A person must not contravene subsection (1).
Penalty: Imprisonment for 12 months.
Subject to subsection (5), the owner, or the person in charge, of:
premises entered under a warrant; or
an aircraft, vehicle or vessel stopped under section 403;

must, if requested by an authorised officer to do so, provide reasonable assistance to the authorised officer in the performance of the functions, or carrying out of the duties, or the exercise of the powers, conferred on the authorised officer under this Act.
A person must not contravene subsection (3).
Penalty: Imprisonment for 12 months.
Where an authorised officer (subject to subsection (6)) makes a request of a person under this section, the authorised officer must:
in the case of a member of a police force—produce, for inspection by that person, written evidence of the fact that he or she is a member of that police force; or
in the case of an officer of Customs—produce, for inspection by that person, written evidence of the fact that he or she is an officer of Customs; or
in any other case—produce his or her identity card for inspection by that person;
and, if the authorised officer fails to do so, that person is not obliged to comply with the request.
Subsection (5) does not apply to an authorised officer if:
the authorised officer is a member of a police force or an officer of Customs; and
the officer is in uniform.

division.heading: Power to search goods, baggage etc.

section.heading: Power to search goods, baggage etc.

content.p: This section applies to any goods that are to be, are being, or have been, taken on or off a ship that voyages, or an aircraft that flies, between:
a place in Australia and a place outside Australia; or
a place in an external Territory and a place outside that Territory.
If an authorised officer believes, on reasonable grounds that goods are goods to which this section applies, he or she may:
examine the goods; or
if the goods are baggage—open and search the baggage; or
if the goods are in a container—open and search the container.

An authorised officer may ask a person who owns, is carrying or is otherwise associated with, or appears to the authorised officer to be associated with, goods to which this section applies any question in respect of the goods.
A person must not refuse or fail to answer a question put to the person under subsection (3).
Penalty: 60 penalty units.
In this Act:
baggage includes any parcel or other goods that:
a passenger; or
the master, a mate, an engineer or any other member of the crew of a ship; or
the pilot or any other member of the crew of an aircraft;
has had with him or her on the ship or aircraft.
goods includes baggage.

division.heading: Power to ask questions about specimens

section.heading: Authorised officer may ask questions about the nature or origin of specimens

content.p: When section applies
This section applies if an authorised officer has reasonable grounds to suspect that:
a specimen has been exported, or is proposed to be exported, in contravention of section 303CC or 303DD; or
a specimen has been imported, or is proposed to be imported, in contravention of section 303CD or 303EK; or
a person has in the person’s possession a specimen, and that possession contravenes section 303GN.
Note: Sections 303CC, 303CD, 303DD, 303EK and 303GN are included in Part 13A, which deals with international movement of wildlife specimens.
Questions

If the authorised officer has reasonable grounds to suspect that a person has information about the nature or origin of the specimen, the authorised officer may ask the person one or more questions about the nature or origin of the specimen.
The authorised officer may ask the questions:
in any case—by asking them in the presence of the person; or
if the authorised officer is not a member of a police force and is not an officer of Customs—by sending written questions to the person.
Answers to questions

Subject to subsections (6) and (7), if a person is asked a question under subsection (2), the person must not intentionally refuse or intentionally fail to answer the question to the extent that the person is capable of doing so.
A person who contravenes subsection (3) commits an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding 10 penalty units.
In subsection (3), strict liability applies to the circumstance that the person was asked a question under subsection (2).
Note: For strict liability, see section 6.1 of the Criminal Code.
No requirement to give incriminating answers
If a person is asked a question under subsection (2), the person is not required to answer the question if the answer might tend to incriminate the person or expose the person to a penalty.
Identity cards etc.
If a person is asked a question under subsection (2) by an authorised officer, the person is not required to answer the question unless:

if the authorised officer is a member of a police force—the authorised officer produces, for inspection by the person, written evidence of the fact that the authorised officer is a member of that police force; or
if the authorised officer is an officer of Customs—the authorised officer produces, for inspection by the person, written evidence of the fact that the authorised officer is an officer of Customs; or
if the authorised officer is not a member of a police force and is not an officer of Customs:
if the questions are asked in the presence of the person—the authorised officer produces the authorised officer’s identity card for inspection by the person; or
if the questions are asked by sending written questions to the person—the authorised officer sends with the questions a copy of his or her instrument of appointment.

division.heading: Power to ask for names and addresses

section.heading: Authorised person may ask for person’s name and address

content.p: An authorised officer may ask an individual to tell the authorised officer the individual’s name and address if the authorised officer has reasonable grounds to suspect that the individual has been involved in the commission of an offence against an environmental law.
Subject to subsection (4), a person must not refuse or fail to comply with a request under subsection (1).
Penalty: 10 penalty units.
A person commits an offence punishable upon conviction by a fine not exceeding 10 penalty units if the person:
in purported compliance with a request under subsection (1), gives a name and address; and
does so knowing the name or address is false or misleading.
If an authorised officer makes a request of a person under subsection (1), the person is not required to comply with the request unless:
if the authorised officer is a member of a police force—he or she produces, for inspection by the person, written evidence of the fact that he or she is a member of that police force; or
if the authorised officer is an officer of Customs—he or she produces, for inspection by the person, written evidence of the fact that he or she is an officer of Customs; or
in any other case—the authorised officer produces his or her identity card for inspection by the person.

subDivision.heading: Seizure of specimens involved in a contravention of Part 13A

section.heading: Seizure of specimens involved in a contravention of Part 13A

content.p: An authorised officer may seize a specimen if he or she has reasonable grounds to suspect that the specimen has been used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against Part 13A.
Note: Part 13A deals with international movement of wildlife specimens.
If a warrant has been issued under Division 4:
if the warrant relates to premises—this section does not apply:
to the executing officer, or an officer assisting, while he or she is searching premises under the warrant; or
to anything found during the course of such a search; and
if the warrant relates to a person—this section does not apply:
to the executing officer, or an officer assisting, while he or she is searching a person, or an aircraft, vehicle or vessel, under the warrant; or
to anything found during the course of such a search.
Note: Division 4 is about search warrants. The Division contains its own seizure powers (see paragraphs 417(1)(c), (d) and (e) and (2)(b), (c) and (d)).

section.heading: Notice about seizure

content.p: Subject to subsection (2), if a specimen is seized by an authorised officer under section 444A, the authorised officer must give:
the owner of the specimen; or
the person who had possession, custody or control of the specimen immediately before it was seized;
a written notice:
identifying the specimen; and
stating that it has been seized under section 444A and giving the reason for the seizure; and
setting out the terms of sections 444C and 444D.
The notice must be given as soon as practicable after the seizure.

An authorised officer is not required to give a notice under subsection (1) about a specimen if, after making such inquiries as the authorised officer thinks appropriate, the authorised officer does not, within 30 days after the seizure, have sufficient information to enable the authorised officer to give the notice. In that event, the authorised officer must keep a written record of the seizure.

section.heading: Applications for return of specimen

content.p: If a specimen is seized under section 444A, the owner of the specimen may apply in writing to the CEO for the delivery to the owner of the specimen.
The application must be made:
within 30 days after the seizure; or
if a notice is given under subsection 444B(1) in relation to the specimen—within 30 days after the giving of the notice.
The application must be made on the ground that the specimen was not used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against Part 13A.
If the applicant satisfies the CEO that the ground has been established, the CEO must grant the application.
Note: Under section 444G, the CEO may retain the specimen for up to 30 days after making a decision on the application.

section.heading: Court action for return of specimen

content.p: If a specimen is seized under section 444A, the owner of the specimen may bring an action against the Commonwealth in a court of competent jurisdiction for the delivery of the specimen to the owner on the ground that the specimen was not used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against Part 13A.
An action under subsection (1) must be brought:
within 30 days after the seizure; or
if a notice is given under subsection 444B(1) in relation to the specimen—within 30 days after the giving of the notice.
If:
an action is brought under subsection (1); and
the court finds that the specimen was used or otherwise involved in the commission of the offence concerned;
the court must order the specimen to be forfeited to the Commonwealth.
If:
an action is brought under subsection (1); and
the action is discontinued by the owner otherwise than because of:
the delivery of the specimen to the owner; or
the forfeiture of the specimen to the Commonwealth; or
the disposal of the specimen under section 449;
the specimen is forfeited to the Commonwealth.

section.heading: Consignment of specimen with consent of owner

content.p: If:
a specimen is seized under section 444A; and
the specimen was imported from a particular foreign country; and
the export of the specimen from the foreign country was not in contravention of a law of the foreign country that corresponds to Part 13A; and
if the importer had applied for a permit authorising the import of the specimen, there is no reasonable likelihood that the permit would have been granted; and
the importer produces written evidence from the relevant CITES authority of the foreign country that the specimen may be returned to the foreign country without contravening such a law;
the CEO may, with the consent of the owner of the specimen, consign the specimen to a place in the foreign country.
The consignment is to be at the expense of the owner of the specimen.

section.heading: Retention of specimen

content.p: If a specimen is seized under section 444A, the specimen may be retained until the end of 30 days after whichever is the latest of the following events:
the seizure;
if a notice is given under subsection 444B(1) in relation to the specimen—the giving of the notice;
if an application is made under subsection 444C(1) in relation to the specimen—the making of a decision on that application;
if:
proceedings for an offence against Part 13A are instituted during the period within which an application may be made under subsection 444C(1) in relation to the specimen; and
the specimen may have been used or otherwise involved in the commission of the offence or the specimen may afford evidence of the commission of the offence;
the termination of the proceedings (including any appeal to a court in relation to those proceedings).
The rule in subsection (1) does not authorise the retention of the specimen if the owner of the specimen succeeds in an action under subsection 444D(1) for the delivery of the specimen to the owner.

As soon as practicable after the end of the period during which the specimen may be retained under subsection (1), the CEO must cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the specimen to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
Subsection (3) does not apply if:
the specimen is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth; or

the specimen has been dealt with under this Part, or as otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory), in a way that means the CEO is not in a position to cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the specimen; or

the Commonwealth, the CEO or an authorised officer is otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory) to retain, destroy, dispose of or otherwise deal with the specimen; or
proceedings under subsection 444D(1) relating to the specimen are pending.

section.heading: Forfeiture of specimen after end of retention period

content.p: If:
a specimen is seized under section 444A; and
none of the following happens before the end of the period for which the specimen may be retained:
proceedings are instituted for an offence against Part 13A, where the specimen is alleged to have been used or otherwise involved in the commission of the offence;
the specimen is released unconditionally to a person under section 449BA;
the specimen is delivered to a person under section 444C;
the owner of the specimen brings an action under subsection 444D(1) for the delivery of the specimen to the owner;
proceedings are instituted under section 450A in relation to the specimen;
the specimen is disposed of under section 449;
the specimen is forfeited to the Commonwealth at the end of that period.
Subsection (1) has effect only to the extent (if any) to which it gives effect to paragraph 1(b) of Article VIII of CITES.

subDivision.heading: Seizure of things (other than specimens involved in a contravention of Part 13A)

section.heading: Seizure of things (other than specimens involved in a contravention of Part 13A)

content.p: Subject to subsections (2) and (3), an authorised officer may seize a thing if he or she has reasonable grounds to suspect that it is evidential material in relation to an offence against an environmental law, in relation to a contravention of an environmental penalty provision or in relation to both.
This section does not apply to a specimen that an authorised officer has reasonable grounds to suspect has been used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against Part 13A.
Note: Section 444A deals with the seizure of such specimens.
If a warrant has been issued under Division 4:
if the warrant relates to premises—this section does not apply:
to the executing officer, or an officer assisting, while he or she is searching premises under the warrant; or
to anything found during the course of such a search; and
if the warrant relates to a person—this section does not apply:
to the executing officer, or an officer assisting, while he or she is searching a person, or an aircraft, vehicle or vessel, under the warrant; or
to anything found during the course of such a search.
Note: Division 4 is about search warrants. The Division contains its own seizure powers (see paragraphs 417(1)(c), (d) and (e) and (2)(b), (c) and (d)).
(3A) A reference in this section to an offence against an environmental law does not include an offence against Part VIIA of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 (compulsory pilotage).
In this section:
thing includes a vehicle, vessel, aircraft, platform, document, organism and specimen.

section.heading: Retention of things seized under this Subdivision

content.p: This section applies to a thing that is seized under section 445.
(1A) The thing may be retained until:
the reason for the seizure no longer exists; or
it is decided that the thing is not to be used in evidence; or
the end of the period of 60 days after the seizure, or, if that period has been extended under subsection (3), the end of the extended period;
whichever happens first.

(1B) As soon as practicable after the end of the period (the retention period) during which the thing may be retained under subsection (1A), the CEO must cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
Subsection (1B) does not apply if:
the thing is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth; or

a proceeding in respect of which the thing may afford evidence was commenced before the end of the retention period and has not been completed (including an appeal to a court in relation to that proceeding); or

the thing has been dealt with under this Part, or as otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory), in a way that means the CEO is not in a position to cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing; or

the Commonwealth, the CEO or an authorised officer is otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory) to retain, destroy, dispose of or otherwise deal with the thing.
An authorised officer may, before the end of the retention period, apply to a magistrate for an order permitting the retention of the thing for a further period.
If, in relation to an application under subsection (2), the magistrate is satisfied, by information on oath or affirmation, that it is necessary for the thing to continue to be retained:
for the purposes of an investigation as to whether an offence against an environmental law has been committed, or whether an environmental penalty provision has been contravened; or

to enable evidence of an offence against an environmental law, or of a contravention of an environmental penalty provision, to be secured for the purposes of a proceeding against the person for such an offence or contravention;
the magistrate may order that the thing may continue to be retained for a period specified in the order. The maximum period of an individual extension must not be more than 30 days.
Before an authorised officer makes an application under subsection (2), he or she must:
take reasonable steps to discover who has an interest in the retention of the thing; and
if it is practicable to do so, give notice in writing of the proposed application to each person whom the authorised officer believes to have an interest in the proposed application.
Subsection (3) does not prevent a magistrate from granting 2 or more successive extensions under that subsection of the period during which the thing may be retained.
A function of making an order conferred on a magistrate by subsection (3) is conferred on the magistrate in a personal capacity and not as a court or a member of a court.
Without limiting the generality of subsection (5), an order made by a magistrate under subsection (3) has effect only by virtue of this Act and is not taken, by implication, to be made by a court.

A magistrate performing a function of, or connected with, making an order under subsection (3) has the same protection and immunity as if he or she were performing that function as, or as a member of, a court (being the court of which the magistrate is a member).

The Governor-General may make arrangements with the Governor of a State, the Chief Minister for the Australian Capital Territory or the Administrator of the Northern Territory for the performance, by all or any of the persons who from time to time hold office as magistrates in that State or Territory, of the function of making orders under subsection (3).

section.heading: Direction to deliver seizable items

content.p: An authorised officer may direct a person to deliver to the officer, or to another person specified in the direction, a thing that the officer is authorised to seize under a warrant issued under Division 4 or under section 445.
The direction must:
be in writing; and
be given to the person who is directed to deliver the thing, who must be:
if the thing is a vessel—the person in charge of the vessel, or the vessel’s owner; or
if the thing is an aircraft—the person in charge of the aircraft; or
otherwise—the person in possession of the thing; and
specify the place at which the delivery is to occur; and
specify the period within which the delivery is to occur.
A person must not fail to comply with a direction under this section.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 12 months or 60 penalty units, or both.
This Part applies to a thing delivered in compliance with a direction under this section as if the thing had been seized under the warrant or section that authorised the officer to seize the thing.
A direction made under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Immediate disposal of seized items

content.p: If:
a thing is seized under this Part; and
the CEO considers that it is reasonably likely that the retention of the thing would:
constitute a serious threat to the environment; or
constitute a serious threat to the continued existence, in the wild, of a particular species of animal or of a particular species of plant; or
result in the introduction of an alien species that represents a threat to ecosystems, habitats or other species; or
constitute a danger to public health; or
in the case of a live organism or specimen—constitute a significant threat to the health of the organism or specimen; or
in the case of a live animal—result in the animal suffering;
the CEO may cause the thing to be dealt with in such manner as the CEO considers appropriate (including the destruction of the thing).
If the CEO causes a live animal to be destroyed under subsection (1), the CEO must require the destruction to be carried out in a humane manner.
Subject to subsection (3), if a thing is dealt with in accordance with subsection (1), the CEO must give to:
the owner of the thing; or
the person who had possession, custody or control of the thing immediately before it was seized;
a written notice:
identifying the thing; and
stating that the thing has been seized under this Part and giving the reason for the seizure; and
stating that the thing has been dealt with under subsection (1) and specifying the manner in which it has been so dealt with and the reason for doing so; and
setting out the terms of subsection (4).
The notice must be given as soon as practicable after the thing is so dealt with.

The CEO need not give a notice under subsection (2) about a thing if, after making such inquiries as the CEO thinks appropriate, the CEO does not, within 20 days after dealing with the thing, have sufficient information to enable the notice to be given.

If a thing is dealt with in accordance with subsection (1), the owner of the thing may bring an action against the Commonwealth in a court of competent jurisdiction for the recovery of the market value of the thing at the time it was so dealt with. The action must be brought on the ground that the thing was not used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against this Act or the regulations.

section.heading: Disposal of seized items if CEO cannot locate or identify person entitled etc.

content.p: This section applies to a thing that is seized under this Part if:
apart from this section, the thing is required to be returned or delivered to a person (or reasonable steps are required to be taken for the return or delivery to a person of the thing); and
one or more of the following applies:
the CEO is satisfied that reasonable steps have been taken to locate or identify the person, but those steps have not succeeded;
the CEO is satisfied that reasonable steps have been taken to return or deliver the thing to the person, but those steps have not succeeded;
the CEO is otherwise satisfied that it is not practicable to return or deliver the thing to the person.
The CEO may dispose of the thing in such manner as the CEO considers appropriate.

subDivision.heading: Release of seized items to owner etc.

section.heading: Release of seized items to owner etc.

content.p: If a thing is seized under this Part, the CEO may authorise the thing, or anything in, on or attached to the thing, to be released to its owner, or to the person from whose possession it was seized, either:
unconditionally; or
on such conditions as the CEO thinks fit (including conditions about the giving of security for giving payment of its value if it is forfeited).
A person commits an offence if:
a thing is released to the person under subsection (1) subject to a condition; and
the person engages in conduct; and
the conduct contravenes the condition.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 12 months or 60 penalty units, or both.
Absolute liability applies to paragraph (2)(a).
Note: For absolute liability, see section 6.2 of the Criminal Code.

section.heading: How this Part applies in relation to things released conditionally

content.p: (1) This section applies if a thing, or anything in, on or attached to a thing, seized under this Part is released on conditions to a person under section 449BA. The provision of this Part under which the seizure was made is the seizure provision, and the thing that is released is the released thing.
Subject to this section, the provisions of this Part that apply in relation to things seized under the seizure provision continue to apply to the released thing as if it had not been released.

A reference in a provision of this Part to the return or delivery of the released thing to a person is, if the person is the person to whom the thing has been released, taken to be a reference to making the release of the thing to the person unconditional.
The regulations may specify modifications of provisions of this Part that are to have effect in relation to things to which this section applies. However, regulations must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.

section.heading: Court-ordered forfeiture: order by court dealing with offence proceedings

content.p: If a court convicts a person of an offence against an environmental law, the court may order the forfeiture to the Commonwealth of any thing used or otherwise involved in the commission of the offence.
If a court convicts a person of an offence against Part 13A, the court must order the forfeiture to the Commonwealth of any specimen used or otherwise involved in the commission of the offence.
Note: Part 13A deals with the international movement of wildlife specimens.
A court may make an order under subsection (1) or (1A) even if the thing or specimen has been seized under this Act or taken into possession under section 406AA or Schedule 1.
If:
a specimen is seized under this Part; and
either:
a court finds a person not guilty of an offence against an environmental law in relation to the specimen; or
a proceeding in a court for such an offence in relation to the specimen is discontinued or dismissed; and

the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that, if the specimen were released to the person from whom it was seized or to its owner, the possession of the specimen by that person would contravene a provision of an environmental law;
the court may order the forfeiture to the Commonwealth of the specimen.
(4) A reference in this section to an offence against an environmental law does not include an offence against Part VIIA of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 (compulsory pilotage).

section.heading: Court-ordered forfeiture: other situations

content.p: A court may, on the application of the CEO, order the forfeiture to the Commonwealth of a thing that is seized under this Part if the court is satisfied that the thing has been used or otherwise involved in the commission of an offence against an environmental law.
Without limiting subsection (1), a court may, on the application of the CEO, order the forfeiture to the Commonwealth of a specimen if:
the specimen was seized under this Part; and
either:
a court has found a person not guilty of an offence against an environmental law in relation to the specimen; or
a proceeding in a court for such an offence in relation to the specimen has been discontinued or dismissed; and

the court to which the CEO applies is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that, if the specimen were released to the person from whom it was seized or to its owner, the possession of the specimen by that person would contravene a provision of an environmental law.
(3) A reference in this section to an offence against an environmental law does not include an offence against Part VIIA of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 (compulsory pilotage).

section.heading: Forfeiture of seized items by consent etc.

content.p: If:
a thing is seized under this Part; and
the owner of the thing agrees to transfer ownership of the thing to the Commonwealth, either:
unconditionally; or
in the event that a future contingency happens; and
if subparagraph (b)(ii) applies—that contingency happens;
then:
the thing becomes the property of the Commonwealth; and
the provisions of this Part relating to forfeiture apply as if the thing had been forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act.
If:
a thing is seized under this Part; and
the owner of the thing agrees to transfer ownership of the thing to the Commonwealth in the event that a future contingency happens;
the CEO may retain the thing:
until the thing becomes the property of the Commonwealth; or
if the thing does not become the property of the Commonwealth—until the end of the last day on which that contingency could happen.
Subsection (2) has effect despite anything in section 438, 444G, 446, 456AB or 456AC.

section.heading: Dealings in forfeited items

content.p: A thing forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act becomes the property of the Commonwealth.
A thing forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act is to be dealt with in such manner as the CEO considers appropriate.
Without limiting subsection (2), the CEO may sell a thing forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act.
The CEO must not sell a specimen forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act unless, in the opinion of the CEO, the buyer will use the specimen for scientific or educational purposes.

section.heading: Delivery of forfeited items to the Commonwealth

content.p: If:
a thing is forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act; and
the thing has not been dealt with under section 451; and
the thing is in the possession, custody or control of a person other than:
the Commonwealth; or
an agency of the Commonwealth; and
the CEO requests the person to deliver the thing to the CEO;
the person must deliver the thing to the CEO.
A person must not contravene subsection (1).
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years.

subDivision.heading: Keeping of organisms or specimens that have been seized

section.heading: Keeping of organisms or specimens retained under this Part

content.p: If a person is authorised under this Part to retain an organism or specimen, the person may do so by causing the organism or specimen to be taken to, and kept at, a place approved by the CEO for the purpose of keeping organisms or specimens seized under this Division.

section.heading: Recovery of costs of storing or keeping organisms or specimens

content.p: If an organism or specimen is seized under this Division, the owner is liable to pay to the Commonwealth an amount equal to the sum of the following costs:
reasonable costs incurred by the Commonwealth in relation to the custody of the organism or specimen;
reasonable costs incurred by the Commonwealth in transporting the organism or specimen;
reasonable costs incurred by the Commonwealth in maintaining the organism or specimen.
If:
an organism or specimen is seized under this Division; and
the organism or specimen is disposed of;
the owner is liable to pay to the Commonwealth an amount equal to the reasonable costs incurred by the Commonwealth in disposing of the organism or specimen.
An amount payable by a person under this section is a debt due by the person to the Commonwealth.
An amount payable by a person to the Commonwealth under this section may be recovered by action in a court of competent jurisdiction.
The CEO may remit an amount payable by a person under this section.

In addition to its effect apart from this subsection, this section also has the effect it would have if a liability under this section were, by express provision, confined to the case of an organism or specimen that:
is forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act; or
would have been forfeited to the Commonwealth under this Act if it had not been disposed of.

section.heading: Rescuing things

content.p: A person commits an offence punishable upon conviction by imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years if:
the person rescues any thing; and
the thing has been, or is about to be, seized under this Act.

section.heading: Breaking or destroying things or documents to prevent seizure etc.

content.p: A person must not:
stave, break or destroy any thing in order to prevent the seizure of a thing, the securing of a thing, or the proof of any offence under an environmental law; or
destroy any documents relating to any thing in order to prevent the seizure of a thing, the securing of a thing, or the proof of any offence under an environmental law.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years.

section.heading: Power to seize cages or containers containing seizable things

content.p: This section applies if:
(a) an authorised officer has power to seize a thing (a seizable thing) under another provision of this Part; and
the seizable thing is in a cage or container; and
the authorised officer considers that it is not reasonably practicable to seize the seizable thing without also seizing the cage or container.

For the purpose of seizing the seizable thing and despite any other provision of this Part, the authorised officer may seize the cage or container containing the seizable thing (whether or not the cage or container also contains any other thing).
The seizure of the seizable thing is taken to occur under the provision mentioned in paragraph (1)(a) (not under this section).

Note: The provisions governing the retention and return of the seizable thing are therefore the provisions that usually govern the seizure of a thing under the provision mentioned in paragraph (1)(a).
If:
an authorised officer seizes a cage or container; and
the seizure of the cage or container is authorised by this section, and is also authorised by another provision of this Part;
then the seizure is taken be under this section, rather than under that other provision (subject to subsection 456AB(5)).

section.heading: Retention of seized cage or container

content.p: This section applies to a cage or container that is seized under section 456AA because it contains a seizable thing.
The cage or container may be retained for so long as an authorised officer considers that it is reasonably necessary to retain it for the purpose of housing the seizable thing.

As soon as practicable after the end of the period during which the cage or container may be retained under subsection (2), the CEO must cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the cage or container to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
Subsection (3) does not apply if:
(a) the seizure was also authorised by another provision of this Part (the other seizure provision), as mentioned in subsection 456AA(4)); or
the cage or container is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth; or

the cage or container has been dealt with under this Part, or as otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory), in a way that means the CEO is not in a position to cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the cage or container; or

the Commonwealth, the CEO or an authorised officer is otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory) to retain, destroy, dispose of or otherwise deal with the cage or container.

If, because of paragraph (4)(a), the cage or container does not have to be returned at the end of the period referred to in subsection (3), this Part then applies in relation to the cage or container as if, at the end of that period, it had been seized under the other seizure provision.

section.heading: Retention of non-seizable things contained in seized cages or containers

content.p: This section applies if:
a cage or container is seized under section 456AA because it contains a seizable thing; and
(b) the cage or container also contains a thing (a non-seizable thing) that is not a seizable thing.
The non-seizable thing may be retained until it is reasonably practicable to return the thing to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).

As soon as practicable after the end of the period during which the non-seizable thing may be retained under subsection (2), the CEO must cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing to the person from whom it was seized (or to the owner if that person is not entitled to possess it).
Subsection (3) does not apply if:
the non-seizable thing is forfeited or forfeitable to the Commonwealth; or

the non-seizable thing has been dealt with under this Part, or as otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory), in a way that means the CEO is not in a position to cause reasonable steps to be taken to return the thing; or

the Commonwealth, the CEO or an authorised officer is otherwise authorised (by a law, or an order of a court, of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory) to retain, destroy, dispose of or otherwise deal with the non-seizable thing.
Subdivision A—Directed environmental audits

section.heading: Directed environmental audits

content.p: (1) The CEO may, by notice in writing to a person in the circumstances set out in subsection (2) or (3), require the person to conduct an environmental audit (a directed environmental audit).
Circumstances in which environmental audit may be required
The circumstances are that:
the person:
is the holder of, or is otherwise approved to take an action under, an environmental authority; or
is subject to an environmental order; or
is a person to whom an environmental exemption applies; and
the CEO reasonably suspects that the person has contravened, or is likely to contravene, a condition or requirement of the authority, order or exemption.
The circumstances are that:
the person:
is the holder of, or is otherwise approved to take an action under, an environmental authority; or
is a person to whom an environmental exemption applies; and
the CEO reasonably suspects that:

the action to which the authority or exemption relates has, has had or is likely to have impacts on the matter dealt with by a provision for which the authority authorises the action or from which the exemption exempts the action; and

those impacts are significantly greater than was indicated in the information available to the person who granted the authority or exemption when it was granted or the person who approved a variation (however described) of the authority or exemption when the variation was approved (if any).
Requirements for notice
The notice must specify:
the matters to be covered by the audit; and
the form of the audit report and the kinds of particulars it is to contain; and
the day on or before which the report must be given to the CEO; and
any other matters prescribed by the regulations.
Without limiting the matters that may be specified for the purposes of paragraph (4)(a), those matters may include all or any of the following:

an evaluation of the nature of the environment that is or will be affected by the activities, of the person, to which the environmental authority, environmental exemption or environmental order is relevant;
an assessment of the risks to the environment resulting from those activities;
an assessment of the person’s existing capacity, in carrying on those activities, to comply with:
for an environmental authority or environmental exemption—any conditions of the authority or exemption; and
for an environmental order—the order; and
in any case—the requirements of this Act and the regulations;
an assessment of what the person will need to do, or continue to do, in order to comply.

section.heading: Appointment of auditor and conducting an audit

content.p: (1) A person who is given notice under section 458 (the audited person) must:
appoint a person to conduct the audit required by the notice; and
(b) arrange for the person appointed (the auditor) to conduct the audit in accordance with the notice.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
The person appointed to conduct the audit must be:
a registered auditor; or
if no registered auditor is reasonably available to conduct the audit—a person who the CEO has approved for such appointment before the appointment is made.
The CEO may, in writing, approve a person for the purposes of paragraph (2)(b) if:
the person approved is not an officer or employee of the audited person; and
the CEO is satisfied that the person approved has the independence, and the knowledge or experience, necessary to properly conduct the audit.
An appointment of a person to conduct the audit made otherwise than in accordance with subsection (2) has no effect.
An approval under subsection (3) is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Nature of directed environmental audit

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person is the auditor for a directed environmental audit; and
in the course of conducting the audit, the person does not deal with a particular matter; and
the matter is specified in the notice under section 458 as a matter that is to be covered by the audit.
Penalty: 30 penalty units.
A person commits an offence if:
the person is the auditor for a directed environmental audit; and
in the course of conducting the audit, the person conceals, or does not take into account, any information or document; and
the information or document is relevant to the audit.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 6 months.

The auditor for a directed environmental audit may have regard to the results of a previous environmental audit, including such an audit conducted in accordance with a condition or requirement of an environmental authority or environmental order to which the audit relates, if:
the previous audit was completed within the last preceding 2 years; and
the auditor is satisfied that the previous audit is still relevant.

section.heading: Audit reports

content.p: After completing a directed environmental audit, the auditor must prepare, and give to the audited person, a written report that:
sets out the results of the audit; and
is in the form, and contains the particulars, specified for the purposes of paragraph 458(4)(b).
Note: A person may commit an offence if the person provides false or misleading information or documents (see sections 137.1 and 137.2 of the Criminal Code).
The audited person must give the report to the CEO:
on or before the day specified by the CEO under paragraph 458(4)(c); or
on or before such later day as the CEO, on application by the audited person, determines in writing.
A person commits an offence if:
the person is required to give the CEO a report under subsection (2); and
the person fails to comply with the requirement.
Penalty for contravention of this subsection: 50 penalty units.
Subdivision B—Compliance audits

section.heading: Compliance audits

content.p: (1) The CEO may, in writing, require an audit (a compliance audit) to be conducted of activities mentioned in column 1 of an item of the following table in relation to any of the matters mentioned in column 2 of the item.

tr.th: Matters for compliance audits
Matters for compliance audits
Matters for compliance audits

tr.td: Column 2 Matters to which audit may relate
Activities purportedly covered by an environmental authority
Activities purportedly covered by an environmental exemption
Activities that: (a) are purportedly carried out for the purposes of complying with an environmental order; or (b) are subject to any requirement of an environmental order
Activities purportedly covered by a marine park permission
Activities that: (a) are purportedly carried out for the purposes of complying with a marine park order; or (b) are subject to any requirement of a marine park order
Activities of a kind prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this item
Any matters that: (a) relate to compliance with an environmental law; and (b) are prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this item

content.p: The audit may deal with anything that is:
reasonably necessary for the effective conduct of the audit; or
incidental to any matters to which the audit relates.

section.heading: Single audit or program of audits may be required

content.p: The CEO may require, under section 462, a single audit, or a program of audits, to be conducted in relation to a specified matter or matters included in a specified class of matters.

Note: If the CEO has required a program of audits to be conducted in relation to a matter, the CEO may also require additional audits to be conducted in relation to the matter (see subsection 33(1) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901).

section.heading: Who may conduct compliance audit

content.p: A compliance audit must be conducted by:
an authorised officer; or
a registered auditor.
(2) The person conducting the audit is the auditor for the audit.

section.heading: Relevant person for a compliance audit

content.p: (1) A person is a relevant person for a compliance audit if the person is:
for an audit of activities relating to an environmental authority:
the holder of the authority; or
if the activities are those of a person who is otherwise approved to take an action under the authority—the person carrying on those activities; or
for an audit of activities relating to an environmental exemption—the person to whom the exemption applies; or
for an audit of activities relating to a marine park permission—the holder of the permission; or
for an audit of activities relating to an environmental order or a marine park order—the person who is subject to the order and whose activities the audit is concerned with; or
for an audit of activities mentioned in item 6 of the table in subsection 462(1)—the person who is or was carrying on, or is proposing to carry on, the activities.

(2) A person is also a relevant person for a compliance audit if the person is acting as an agent of the relevant person under subsection (1), and appears to be doing or to have done so in relation to activities to which the audit relates.

section.heading: Conduct of audit

content.p: The CEO need not give notice of a compliance audit.
Before starting to conduct a compliance audit, the auditor for the audit:
must give a description of the scope of the audit to the relevant person for the audit under subsection 462C(1); and

must take reasonable steps to give such a description to any relevant person for the audit under subsection 462C(2) whose assistance the auditor considers will be reasonably necessary for the conduct of the audit (see section 462E).
Regulations may make provision in relation to other matters
The regulations may make provision for and in relation to:
other matters relating to the conduct of a compliance audit; and
the process to be followed after a compliance audit has been completed.
Without limiting subsection (3), the regulations may make provision for and in relation to the following:
information that must be provided to relevant persons for a compliance audit before the audit, during the audit or after the audit is completed;
requirements for reports to be provided in relation to a compliance audit.
Note: A person may commit an offence if the person provides false or misleading information or documents (see sections 137.1 and 137.2 of the Criminal Code).

section.heading: Relevant person must provide assistance

content.p: A person must provide the auditor for a compliance audit with assistance that is reasonably necessary for the conduct of the audit if:
the person is a relevant person for the audit under subsection 462C(1); or
the person is a relevant person for the audit under subsection 462C(2) and the auditor requests the assistance of the person.
Without limiting subsection (1), providing assistance that is reasonably necessary includes complying with any request under subsection 462F(1) for the audit.
Subsection (1) does not require a relevant person for the audit to allow the auditor:
to enter premises; or
to take samples of any thing at premises; or
to inspect any thing at premises.
A person commits an offence if:
the person is a relevant person for a compliance audit; and
the person fails to provide the assistance required by subsection (1) in relation to the audit.
Penalty for contravention of this subsection: 30 penalty units.

section.heading: Powers of auditors

content.p: (1) For the purpose of conducting a compliance audit, the auditor for the audit may request a person who the auditor reasonably believes has information or documents that are relevant to the audit to answer questions, provide information in writing or produce the documents.
Note: A person may commit an offence if the person provides false or misleading information or documents (see sections 137.1 and 137.2 of the Criminal Code).
The auditor may make copies of, or take extracts from, a document or record produced under subsection (1).
Subdivision C—Other matters relating to audits

section.heading: Register of auditors

content.p: The CEO must cause a register of auditors to be kept for the purposes of this Act.
The CEO must register an individual in the register if:
the individual has applied for registration in accordance with regulations made for the purposes of subsection (4); and
the CEO is satisfied that it is appropriate to register the individual as an auditor, having regard to:
the individual’s qualifications, knowledge, expertise, competence and independence; and
any other matters as are prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this subparagraph; and
any other matters the CEO considers relevant.
Note: The CEO may impose conditions on an individual’s registration (see section 462J).
If the CEO is not satisfied that it is appropriate to register the individual as an auditor, the CEO must refuse to register the individual.
The regulations may provide for any of the following:
the form and content of the register;
publication of the register;
the form and content of applications for registration and the manner in which applications are to be made;
fees to be paid in connection with registration (including ongoing or recurrent fees to maintain registration);
requirements to be met in order to maintain registration;
review of registration;
suspension of registration in prescribed circumstances;
deregistration in prescribed circumstances;
inspection of the performance of registered auditors in conducting directed environmental audits;
inspection of the performance of registered auditors in conducting compliance audits;
inspection of the performance of registered auditors in conducting environmental audits required by conditions of approvals under Part 9;
other matters in connection with registration in the register.
A fee under paragraph (4)(d) must not be such as to amount to taxation.
The register is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Registered auditors must comply with guidelines

content.p: A registered auditor must comply with guidelines prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this subsection (if any) in relation to the conduct of a directed environmental audit or a compliance audit.
Note: The consequences of a registered auditor failing to comply with the guidelines are set out in regulations made for the purposes of subsection 462G(4).
Regulations prescribing guidelines

(2) Despite subsection 14(2) of the Legislation Act 2003, regulations made for the purposes of subsection (1) may make provision in relation to a matter by applying, adopting, or incorporating, with or without modification, any matter contained in an instrument or other writing as in force or existing from time to time.
Subsection (2) applies whether or not the instrument or other writing was created for a purpose other than being applied, adopted or incorporated by the regulations.

To the extent that regulations making provision as mentioned in subsection (2) constitutes a subdelegation of the Governor-General’s power to make regulations for the purposes of subsection (1), subsection (2) authorises that subdelegation.

section.heading: Conditions of registration

content.p: The CEO may impose one or more conditions on an individual’s registration as a registered auditor.
Without limiting subsection (1), the CEO may impose conditions setting out the following:
the kinds of audits the individual is able to conduct;
the circumstances in which the individual is able to conduct an audit or a kind of audit;
requirements or restrictions relating to the individual’s independence as a registered auditor.
The regulations may provide for or in relation to any of the following:
the process to be followed in deciding to impose conditions;
notification of such decisions;
review of such decisions;
variation or revocation of conditions;
other matters in connection with conditions.

section.heading: Other audit obligations not affected

content.p: Nothing in this Division affects any obligation of a person to conduct an audit in accordance with a condition or requirement of an environmental authority, environmental exemption, marine park permission, environmental order or marine park order.

section.heading: Simplified outline of this Division

content.p: The following is a simplified outline of this Division:

The Minister may make conservation orders controlling activities, and requiring specified people to take specified actions, in Commonwealth areas to protect listed threatened species or ecological communities.
A person who contravenes a conservation order commits an offence.
Before the Minister makes a conservation order, he or she must consult various Commonwealth agencies.
The Secretary must publicise conservation orders, and may give assistance to a person to comply with a conservation order.

section.heading: Minister may make conservation orders

content.p: Making conservation orders
(1) The Minister may make a written order (a conservation order):
prohibiting or restricting specified activities on or in:
all Commonwealth areas; or
specified Commonwealth areas; or
requiring specified persons to take specified action on or in:
all Commonwealth areas; or
specified Commonwealth areas.
Note: Section 470 makes contravening a conservation order an offence.
Prerequisite to making conservation order

The Minister may only make a conservation order if he or she reasonably believes that it is necessary to make the order to protect a listed threatened species or a listed threatened ecological community.
Minister must consider economic and social matters

In considering whether to make a conservation order, the Minister must be satisfied that making the order is justified, having regard to economic and social considerations that are consistent with the principles of ecologically sustainable development.
Minister must consult before making conservation order
Before making a conservation order, the Minister:
must seek the Secretary’s advice on whether it should be made; and

must consult each Commonwealth agency that may be affected by the order, and any other Commonwealth agency the Minister thinks appropriate, unless delay in making the order would result in significant, irreparable damage to a listed threatened species or listed threatened ecological community.

section.heading: Duration of conservation orders

content.p: A conservation order comes into force:
if a commencement day is specified in the order—on that day; or
otherwise—immediately after it is made.
The order remains in force:
for the period (if any) specified in the order; or
until it is revoked by the Minister.

section.heading: Reviews of conservation orders

content.p: The Minister must:
at intervals of not more than 5 years, review the conservation order; and
after each review, confirm, vary or revoke the order by instrument in writing.
Before reviewing the order, the Minister must seek the Secretary’s advice on the review.

The Minister must not revoke the order unless he or she is satisfied that the order is no longer needed to protect the listed threatened species or listed threatened ecological community the order was made to protect.

The Minister must not vary the order unless he or she is satisfied that the order as varied adequately protects the listed threatened species or listed threatened ecological community the order was first made to protect.
Immediately after a variation of the order, the order continues in force as so varied.

section.heading: Publication of conservation orders

content.p: As soon as practicable after making or reviewing a conservation order, the Minister must cause the Secretary to be informed of the making of the order, or the decision on the review, as the case requires.
The Secretary must, as soon as practicable after being so informed:

(a) cause to be published in the Gazette, in a daily newspaper circulating in each State or self-governing Territory in which are located Commonwealth areas to which the order relates and in any other way required by the regulations, a notice containing:
a copy of the order; and
a statement to the effect that contravention of the order is an offence against this Act; and
if applicable, a statement of the decision on the review; and

a statement to the effect that a person affected by the order may apply to the Minister, within 28 days of the publication (or within such further period as the Minister allows), for a reconsideration of the order by the Minister; and
take all reasonable steps to ensure that each person who the Secretary knows would be affected by the order is given a notice containing:
a copy of the order; and
if applicable, a statement of the decision on the review; and
unless the person is a Commonwealth agency or an agency of a State or self-governing Territory—a statement to the effect that contravention of the order is an offence against this Act; and

a statement to the effect that the person may apply to the Minister, within 28 days of being given the notice (or within such further period as the Minister allows), for a reconsideration of the order by the Minister.
Failure to comply with this section does not affect the validity of the order.

section.heading: Application for reconsideration of conservation orders or decisions on review

content.p: A person affected by a conservation order, or by the decision on a review of a conservation order, may apply to the Minister to reconsider the order or the decision, as the case requires.
The application must be in writing.

Subject to subsection (4), the application must be made within 28 days, or within such further period as the Minister allows, after the publication under paragraph 467(2)(a) of the notice relating to the making of the order or conduct of the review.

If the person is given a copy of the order after that publication, the period of 28 days within which that person must make the application is taken to commence on the day on which the person received the notice.

section.heading: Reconsideration of conservation orders and decisions on review

content.p: Upon receiving the application, the Minister must:
seek the Secretary’s advice on the application; and
reconsider the conservation order or the decision on review, as the case requires; and
by written instrument:
confirm, vary or revoke the order; or
confirm or vary the decision on review; and
cause the Secretary to be informed accordingly.
As soon as practicable after being so informed, the Secretary must:
notify the applicant in writing of the result of the reconsideration; and
(b) if the order is revoked or varied or the decision on review is varied—cause to be published in the Gazette, and in any other way required by the regulations, a notice:
stating that fact; and
in the case of a variation—setting out a copy of the order or decision as so varied.
Immediately after a variation of the order, the order continues in effect as so varied.

section.heading: Contravening conservation orders is an offence

content.p: A person must not take an action reckless as to whether the action contravenes a conservation order.
Penalty: 500 penalty units.

If a person believes that taking an action that he or she proposes to take may contravene a particular conservation order, the person may seek the Minister’s advice under subsection 471(3) on whether the order would be contravened by taking that action.
The person does not contravene the order if he or she acts in accordance with advice given to him or her under subsection 471(3) to the effect that the order would not be contravened.

section.heading: Minister to consider proposed actions etc.

content.p: This section applies to a proposed action if it is referred to the Minister under section 470 for the Minister’s advice on whether it would contravene a conservation order.
A person who proposes to take the action may make written submissions to the Minister about the proposed action.
The Minister must:
refer the proposed action, together with any submissions received by the Minister about the proposed action, to the Secretary; and
after considering the Secretary’s advice on the matter, give the person who sought the Minister’s advice under section 470 a written notice of the minister’s advice on the proposed action.

section.heading: Contents of notices of advice

content.p: The notice of advice must state whether the Minister thinks that the proposed action would contravene a conservation order.
If the decision to give the advice was not made personally by the Minister and the notice of advice is given to a person who is not a Commonwealth agency, the notice must include:

(a) a statement to the effect that, if the person is dissatisfied with the decision to give that advice, application may, subject to the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024, be made to the Administrative Review Tribunal for review of the decision; and
a statement to the effect that the person may request a statement under that Act in relation to the decision.

section.heading: Review by the Administrative Review Tribunal

content.p: Subject to subsections (1A) and (2), applications may be made to the Administrative Review Tribunal for review of the decision to give the advice.
Subsection (1) does not apply to a decision made personally by the Minister (but the subsection does apply to a decision made by a delegate of the Minister).
(2) Despite sections 17 and 35 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024, applications are not to be made by or on behalf of Commonwealth agencies.

section.heading: Assistance in complying with conservation orders

content.p: On behalf of the Commonwealth, the Secretary may provide assistance to a person (other than a Commonwealth agency) to comply with prohibitions, restrictions or requirements imposed on a person by a conservation order.
The assistance may take any one or more of the following forms:
payment of money;
provision of goods;
provision of labour;
provision of other services.
The value of the assistance must not exceed that which the Secretary thinks are the reasonable and direct costs of complying with the prohibitions, restrictions or requirements in question.
Assistance given under this section must be taken into account in determining compensation payable under section 519.

section.heading: CEO may issue environment protection orders

content.p: (1) The CEO may issue an order under this section (an environment protection order) if the CEO reasonably believes that:
a person has engaged, is engaging or is likely to engage in conduct consisting of an act or omission that constitutes:
a contravention of a provision of this Act or the regulations; or
a contravention of one or more conditions of an environmental authority under which the person is approved to take an action; or
a contravention of one or more conditions of an environmental exemption which applies to the person; and
the contravention or likely contravention is causing, or poses an imminent risk of, serious damage to a matter covered by subsection (2); and
it is necessary to issue the order for either or both of the following purposes:
ensuring the person’s future compliance with this Act or the regulations, or the conditions of the environmental authority or environmental exemption;
preventing or mitigating the damage caused, or eliminating or reducing the risk of damage posed, by the contravention or likely contravention to the matter covered by subsection (2).
For the purposes of paragraphs (1)(b) and (c), this subsection covers the following matters:
in relation to a contravention or likely contravention of a provision:
for a provision of Part 3—the matter protected by the provision; or
for any other provision—the environment, to the extent that it is dealt with by the provision;
in relation to a contravention or likely contravention of conditions of an environmental authority or environmental exemption:
for an approval under Part 9—the matter protected by any provision of Part 3 for which the approval has effect; or
for a national interest exemption or continuing section 158 exemption from a provision of Part 3—the matter protected by any provision of Part 3 from which an action is exempt under the exemption; or

for a national interest exemption or continuing section 158 exemption from a provision of Chapter 4—the matter protected by any provision of Part 3 that is, or would be but for the exemption, a controlling provision for the action that is exempt under the exemption; or
for a permit issued under Chapter 5—the environment, to the extent that it is dealt with by any provision of that Chapter for which the permit has effect; or

for a Part 13 exemption or continuing section 303A exemption—the environment, to the extent that it is dealt with by any provision of Part 13 or regulations made under Part 13 from which an action is exempt under the exemption.
The order may impose any requirements on the person that the CEO reasonably believes are necessary for the purposes mentioned in paragraph (1)(c), including by doing any or all of the following:
requiring the person to discontinue or not commence specified activities;
requiring the person to change the manner in which the person is carrying on, or is to carry on, specified activities;
otherwise restricting the manner in which the person is carrying on, or is to carry on, specified activities;
requiring the person to take specified action in a specified manner or in specified circumstances.
How order may be issued
An environment protection order may be issued:
by notice in writing; or
if the CEO is satisfied it is necessary to do so because of urgent circumstances—by notice given orally (including by telephone).
For the purposes of subsection (4), the notice may be:

given to the person to whom the order applies, including, if the notice is given orally and the person is not an individual, by giving the notice to any employee or officer of the person acting in that capacity; or
given to any person who is acting as an agent of the person to whom the order applies in relation to activities to which the order relates.

If the order is issued by notice in writing to an agent mentioned in paragraph (5)(b), the CEO must, within 72 hours after the order is issued, give a copy of the notice to the person to whom the order applies.
If the order is issued by notice given orally to a person, the CEO must, within 72 hours after the oral notice is given:
give notice in writing of the order to the person to whom the order applies; and
if the oral notice was given to an agent mentioned in paragraph (5)(b)—give a copy of the notice in writing of the order to the agent.
Other matters
Neither of the following is a legislative instrument:
an environment protection order issued in writing under paragraph (4)(a);
notice of an environment protection order under subsection (7).

section.heading: Content of environment protection orders

content.p: An environment protection order must (subject to subsection (2)):
state the day on which the order is issued; and
state the name of the person the order applies to; and
state the purposes for which the order is issued, including by giving brief details of any alleged contravention or potential contravention to which the order relates; and
set out the requirements imposed on the person by the order; and
specify that, unless extended, or revoked earlier, the order remains in force until the end of:
the period of 14 days after the day it comes into force; or
a specified shorter period.
If an environment protection order is issued by notice given orally under paragraph 474A(4)(b):

a requirement in subsection (1) of this section for the order to contain a matter is taken to be a requirement for the CEO, when issuing the order, to inform the person to whom notice of the order is given of the matter; and
a reference in this Act or the regulations to a matter specified in the order is taken to be a reference to a matter of which the person has been so informed; and
notice of the environment protection order under subsection 474A(7) must include each matter so informed.

section.heading: Supporting documents

content.p: The CEO must, in accordance with this section, provide the person to whom an environment protection order applies with one or more documents that support the CEO’s reasonable belief as to the matters mentioned in paragraph 474A(1)(a).
If the environment protection order is issued by notice in writing, a copy of the documents must accompany:
the notice; and
if the notice was given to an agent mentioned in paragraph 474A(5)(b)—the copy of the notice required by subsection 474A(6) to be given to the person to whom the order applies.
If the environment protection order is issued by notice given orally, a copy of the documents must accompany:
the notice in writing that is required by paragraph 474A(7)(a) to be given to the person to whom the order applies; and
if the oral notice was given to an agent mentioned in paragraph 474A(5)(b)—the copy of the notice in writing that is required by paragraph 474A(7)(b) to be given to the agent.

section.heading: Duration of environment protection orders

content.p: An environment protection order comes into force immediately after notice of the order is given under subsection 474A(4).
Note: For the persons to whom notice may be given under subsection 474A(4), see subsection (5) of that section.
The order remains in force until the end of the period specified in the order for the purposes of paragraph 474B(1)(e), unless:
the order is extended by a variation made under subsection 474D(1); or
the order is revoked earlier under subsection 474D(1).
